He wrote many philosophical books about faith, existence, emotions, and feeling. He disliked people who tried to make Christianity political and people who tried to limit the single individual in favour of groups of many people. Many people have found his works interesting and have said that they were great works of philosophy. Ludwig Wittgenstein, a 20th-century philosopher, thought Kierkegaard was "by far, the most profound thinker of the nineteenth century". He was born in Copenhagen, Denmark. He attended Copenhagen University and earned his master's degree in 1841. During this time, he met and fell in love with Regine Olsen in 1837. Although they were engaged for a time, Kierkegaard ended the engagement in 1841. After breaking up with Regine, he spent much of his time writing book after book, in a highly dramatic yet subtle way. He also wrote some of his works using pen names, or pseudonyms. He died in Copenhagen. Although his works were not very popular during his lifetime, after his death they became influential in the 20th century. Books by Kierkegaard. Either/Or and Fear and Trembling, both published in 1843, are thought to be especially significant. (1841) The Concept of Irony (Om Begrebet Ironi med stadigt Hensyn til Socrates) (1843) Fear and Trembling (Frygt og Bæven) (1844) Philosophical Fragments (Philosophiske Smuler) (1844) The Concept of Dread (Begrebet Angest) (1845) Stages on Life's Way (Stadier paa Livets Vei) (1846) Concluding Unscientific Postscript to The Philosophical Fragments (Afsluttende uvidenskabelig Efterskrift) (1847) Edifying Discourses in Divers Spirits (1847) Works of Love (Kjerlighedens Gjerninger) (1848) Christian Discourses (Christelige Taler) (1849) The Sickness Unto Death (Sygdommen til Døden) (1850) Training in Christianity (Indøvelse i Christendom)

Gotthold Ephraim Lessing (22 January 1729 in Kamenz (Saxony) – 15 February 1781 in Braunschweig) was a German poet and philosopher in the time of the enlightenment. Lessing was one of twelve children. His father was a Protestant priest. He went to school in Kamenz and got a stipendium for the Higher School in Meißen. From 1746 to 1748, he studied medicine and theology in Leipzig. In 1750, he moved to Berlin, where he met Voltaire. In 1752 he got the Magister (Master) degree from the university in Wittenberg. He moved back to Leipzig in 1755, but returned later to Berlin. He traveled around in Europe and studied. He worked as a reporter. From 1760 to 1765, he worked as secretary for a general in Breslau (today: Wroclaw). Later he worked at the theater and became a librarian. Lessing got married in 1776. But 1778 his wife died. In 1781, Lessing died.

John Locke (; 29 August 1632 – 28 October 1704), known as the Father of Liberalism, was an English philosopher and physician. His writings on the theory of social contract influenced Voltaire and Rousseau, many Scottish Enlightenment thinkers, and the American revolutionaries. His ideas are mentioned in the American Declaration of Independence. Locke's theories were usually about identity and the self. Locke thought that we are born without thoughts, and that knowledge is instead determined only by experience. Locke's father, who was also named John Locke, was a country lawyer. He had served as a captain in the early part of the English Civil War. His mother, Agnes Keene, was a tanner's daughter and was thought to be very beautiful. Both mother and father were Puritans. Locke was born on 29 August 1632, in a cottage by the church in Wrington, Somerset, about twelve miles from Bristol. He was baptized when he was born. After that, his family soon moved to Pensford. In 1647, Locke was sent to Westminster School in London. During this time he was being sponsored by Alexander Popham, a member of the Parliament. After finishing his studies there, he went into the Christ Church. Although Locke was a good student, he did not like the schedule of the time spent there. He did not like the classical subjects taught at the university, and wanted to learn more about modern philosophy. Through his friend Richard Lower, whom he had met at the school, Locke learned about medicine, because his friend Richard Lower taught it to him. Locke was awarded a bachelor's degree in 1656 and a master's degree in 1658. In 1666, he met Lord Anthony Ashley Cooper, who had come to Oxford seeking treatment for his liver disease. Cooper was impressed with Locke and asked him to come. Locke had been looking for a job and in 1667 moved into Shaftesbury's home at Exeter House in London, to serve as Lord Ashley's personal physician. In London, Locke continued his studies on medicine. Locke's medical knowledge was put to the test when Shaftesbury's liver disease became worse until Shaftesbury was about to die. Locke used the advice of several physicians and persuaded Shaftesbury to go to an operation. Shaftesbury lived through the operation and thanked Locke for saving his life. Shaftesbury, as a member of the Whig movement, was a big influence on Locke's political ideas. However, after Shaftesbury began to fall from favor in 1675, Locke decided to travel across France. He came back to England in 1679. At this time, due to Shaftesbury's insistence, Locke wrote the Two Treatises of Government. While it was once thought that Locke wrote the Treatises to defend the Glorious Revolution of 1688, recent scholarship has shown that the work was composed before this even started. However, Locke ran away to the Netherlands in 1683. This is because people became suspicious of him being involved in the Rye House Plot to assassinate King Charles II of England. In the Netherlands, Locke had time to return to his writing, spending a great deal of time re-working the essay. Locke did not return home until after the Glorious Revolution. Locke came with William of Orange's wife back to England in 1688. Locke's close friend Lady Masham invited him to join her at the Mashams' country house in Essex. Although his time there was marked by variable health from asthma attacks, he nevertheless became an intellectual hero of the Whigs. During this period he discussed matters with such figures as John Dryden and Isaac Newton. He died on 28 October 1704, and is buried in the churchyard of the village of High Laver, east of Harlow in Essex, where he had lived in the household of Sir Francis Masham since 1691. Locke never married nor had children. Events that happened during Locke's lifetime include the English Restoration, the Great Plague of London and the Great Fire of London. He did not quite see the Acts of Union 1707 though the thrones of England and Scotland were held in personal union throughout his lifetime. Constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy were in their infancy during Locke's time.

John Stuart Mill (20 May 1806 – 8 May 1873) was an English philosopher and political economist. He was a classical liberal thinker of the 19th century. He was for utilitarianism, the ethical theory first proposed by his godfather Jeremy Bentham. As a utilitarian, he believed that the good of society as a whole is more important than the pleasure of one or a few individuals.

Friedrich Wilhelm Nietzsche was a German philosopher, writer, and scholar of ancient languages. He was born on 15 October 1844 and died on 25 August 1900. Nietzsche studied ancient Greek and Latin writings. He became a professor at the University of Basel in Switzerland when he was 24 years old. After ten years he had to give up his job because he was often sick. For the rest of his working life he had no fixed home. He moved between cheap rooms in Switzerland, Italy, and France, and wrote almost all of his famous books in those years. His books are not like ordinary philosophy books. Many of them are made of short, sharp pieces of writing called aphorisms. He used jokes, stories, and strong images instead of long chains of proof. He attacked Christianity and the common ideas about right and wrong. He said that the old religious view of the world was dying, and he wrote the famous line "God is dead" to describe this. He thought that people would have to find new values for themselves, or fall into the belief that life means nothing. Some of his best known ideas are the will to power, the eternal return of all things, and the Übermensch, which means the "overman" or "overhuman". In January 1889 Nietzsche had a sudden mental breakdown. He never got better. He spent the last eleven years of his life unable to work, cared for first by his mother and then by his sister. He died in 1900, just as his fame was beginning to grow. During his illness and after his death, his sister took more and more control of his writings. She changed how people read him. Later, the German Nazi Party used parts of his work for their own ends, often by taking his words out of their setting. Scholars after the Second World War showed that this picture of Nietzsche was false. He is studied as a thinker who shaped existentialism, modern psychology, and much of later European thought. Nietzsche was born in the village of Röcken, near Lützen, in the eastern part of Germany. His father, Carl Ludwig Nietzsche, was a Lutheran pastor, which is a kind of Christian minister. His father died in 1849, when Friedrich was only four. His baby brother died the next year. After that, the young boy grew up in a house full of women: his mother, his younger sister Elisabeth, his grandmother, and two aunts. In 1850 the family moved to the town of Naumburg. As a boy Nietzsche was serious, careful, and very good at his lessons. From 1858 to 1864 he went to Schulpforta, one of the best and strictest schools in Germany. There he fell in love with the ancient Greek and Latin writers. His family hoped he would become a Christian minister like his father. So he first went to the University of Bonn to study religion. But he quickly gave up religion and moved to the University of Leipzig to study philology, the careful study of old languages and texts. He then read a book by the German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer called The World as Will and Representation. Schopenhauer wrote that the world is controlled by a blind, hungry force he called the "will", and that life is mostly suffering. Nietzsche also started listening to music by the composer Richard Wagner, whom he met in 1868 and admired for years. In April 1869 something rare happened. The University of Basel in Switzerland offered Nietzsche a chair as a professor of classical philology. He was only 24, and he had not even chosen the subject of his doctoral thesis. Leipzig gave him the degree without an exam, because his work was already so respected. He gave his first lecture there in May 1869. To take the job he gave up his Prussian citizenship. He never became a Swiss citizen either, so for the rest of his life he officially belonged to no country. In 1870 a war broke out between Prussia and France. Nietzsche served for a short time as a medical helper, caring for wounded and sick soldiers. He caught serious illnesses himself. From then on his health was never strong. He suffered from terrible headaches, stomach trouble, and very poor eyesight for the rest of his life. His first book came out in 1872. It was called The Birth of Tragedy. In it he wrote about ancient Greek plays and about two forces in art and life, which are explained below. Other scholars of ancient languages harshly criticized the book. Then Nietzsche slowly grew less friendly with Wagner. He thought that Wagner's later music turned toward Christian feeling and German national pride. Nietzsche disliked both. Nietzsche and Wagner stopped being friends. In 1878 Nietzsche published Human, All Too Human, a book of sharp short pieces that questioned many things he had once loved. By 1879 his health was so bad that he had to leave his post at Basel. The university gave him a small pension to live on. The next ten years were hard but full of work. Nietzsche had no home of his own. In summer he often stayed in the cool mountain village of Sils-Maria in Switzerland. In winter he moved to warmer towns such as Nice in France or Genoa and Turin in Italy. In 1881 he published Daybreak, and in 1882 The Gay Science. The phrase "gay science" here means joyful or playful knowledge, not anything to do with sexuality. The year 1882 also brought a painful episode in his private life. He fell in love with a young writer and thinker named Lou Salomé and hoped to marry her. She refused. This unhappy episode belongs to the years in which he began his next and most famous book. That book was Thus Spoke Zarathustra, written between 1883 and 1885. It is part poem, part story, and part prophecy. Its hero, named after an ancient Persian teacher, comes down from a mountain to share his wisdom with people. Through this character Nietzsche set out his ideas about the Übermensch and the eternal return. The year 1888 was the most productive of all. In a single burst Nietzsche wrote The Case of Wagner, Twilight of the Idols, The Antichrist, and Ecce Homo, a strange book about his own life and work. He had never written so much, or so fast. He was also more alone than ever, and almost unknown to the wider public. In early January 1889, in the city of Turin, Nietzsche broke down. According to a famous story, he saw a horse being beaten in the street, threw his arms around its neck, and collapsed. Many writers repeat this story, but it may not be exactly true. What is certain is that his mind gave way. He sent wild letters to friends, signing them with strange names. He was taken to a clinic and never recovered his reason. What caused the breakdown is still debated. For a long time most doctors blamed syphilis, a disease that can attack the brain. Some scholars now doubt this and suggest other causes, such as a slow brain illness. Whatever the reason, the last eleven years of his life were silent ones. His mother cared for him until she died in 1897. After that his sister took him into her house in the German city of Weimar. Friedrich Nietzsche died there on 25 August 1900, aged 55. Nietzsche is hard to sum up, and on purpose. He did not build one neat system in which every idea fits together. He wrote in pieces, he changed his mind, and he often wore "masks", saying one thing to make people think harder about another. He warned readers not to follow him blindly. Because of this, people still argue about what he really meant. The ideas below are the most important and the most discussed. In his first book, The Birth of Tragedy, Nietzsche described two forces that he saw at work in art and in life. He named them after two Greek gods. The first he called the "Apollonian", after Apollo, the god of light, form, and dreams. This is the drive toward order, clear shapes, and calm beauty. Think of a perfect marble statue, or a quiet, well-made painting. The second he called the "Dionysian", after Dionysus, the god of wine and wild feasts. This is the drive toward energy, loss of self, and being swept away. Think of music that makes a crowd move as one, or a dance in which a person forgets who they are. Nietzsche thought that great Greek tragedy joined these two forces together. The wild Dionysian truth, that life is full of pain and chaos, was made bearable by Apollonian beauty and form. Later in his life he leaned more and more toward the Dionysian side. He used the name Dionysus as a sign for saying a full "yes" to life, even to its suffering. One of Nietzsche's deepest projects was to ask where ideas of "good" and "evil" come from. He set this out most clearly in On the Genealogy of Morality (1887). A "genealogy" is a kind of family tree. Nietzsche traced the family tree of moral ideas, to show that they have a history and were not simply handed down from heaven. He described two very different ways of judging the world. He called the first "master morality". Here the strong, proud, and successful look at themselves and call their own qualities "good": strength, courage, health, beauty. Then they call the opposite "bad", meaning weak or low. The starting point is a "yes" to themselves. He called the second "slave morality". This grows among the weak, the ruled, and the suffering. They cannot beat the strong by force, so they fight back in their minds. They call the qualities of the strong "evil", and they make a virtue out of their own state, praising humility, patience, pity, and obedience. Nietzsche thought that this turn was driven by a hidden, helpless anger. He named it with the French word ressentiment. This means a deep and lasting bitterness. Nietzsche gave a famous picture of this in the Genealogy. Imagine birds of prey carrying off little lambs. The lambs may decide that the birds are "evil", and that they, the lambs, who eat no one, are therefore "good". From the lambs' point of view this feels like justice. But, Nietzsche pointed out, it is a little strange to blame a bird of prey for acting like a bird of prey. It is important to read this carefully. Nietzsche was not simply praising cruelty or telling people to be bullies. He studied culture almost like a doctor studies an illness, trying to show where common values came from and what they cost. At the same time, he should not be made too gentle. He really did admire rank, discipline, and the making of higher kinds of human beings, and he attacked the idea that all people are equal. His view of morality cannot be reduced only to "being true to yourself". Nietzsche grew up in a Christian home, and he knew the religion well. As an adult he became one of its sharpest critics. He set out his attack most strongly in The Antichrist (written in 1888). The word "antichrist" here means "against Christ" or "against Christianity". Nietzsche linked Christianity to slave morality. In his view, certain forms of the religion grew out of the hidden resentment of the weak, above all in the way it later hardened into a moral code and a church. He argued that it taught people to feel guilty, to fear the body, and to look away from this life toward a better world after death. In his eyes this turned people against life itself. He called such values "life-denying", meaning that they say "no" to the natural world. Nietzsche also drew a sharp picture of the difference between Jesus and the apostle Paul. This picture was his own reading of the two men as human types. It was not a neutral piece of history. He treated Jesus as a gentle figure who lived a certain inner state. He treated Paul as the man who built a church, and a whole system of guilt and reward, around that figure. It is not a portrait that most scholars of religion would accept. Nietzsche's most famous saying is "God is dead". He did not mean that a living god had died. He meant something about culture and belief. He thought that in the modern world, science and reason had quietly destroyed the old faith in God, even among people who still went to church. In his view, the shared belief that once held everything together was dying out. He gave this idea a striking scene in The Gay Science (section 125). A madman runs into a market square in the morning with a lantern, crying out that he is looking for God. The people there, who no longer believe, only laugh at him. The madman tells them a terrible thing: it is they who have killed God, and they have not yet understood what they have done. For Nietzsche this was not good news to celebrate. He saw a great danger ahead, which he called nihilism. Nihilism is the belief that nothing has any meaning, value, or purpose. If the old source of values is gone, people may feel that life is empty and that nothing matters. Nietzsche thought this was the deepest crisis facing the modern world. His whole work can be read as a search for a way through nihilism, by creating new values out of love for life rather than fear of it. Schopenhauer had said that all living things are driven by a "will to live", a simple wish to survive and to keep going. Nietzsche thought this did not go far enough. He proposed instead a "will to power". Nietzsche often describes life as a drive to grow, to overcome resistance, and to become stronger. A plant pushes through stone toward the light. An artist works for years to master a craft. A thinker tries to understand more and more of the world. In each case the deep urge is not only to stay alive, but to overcome and to expand. This idea is one of the most debated in all of Nietzsche. Some readers take it as a claim about all of nature, almost like a law of physics. Others take it more narrowly, as an idea about human drives and feelings. It is also easy to twist. "Power" here does not only mean armies or rule over others, and it does not only mean quiet self-control either. It covers the full range of striving, growth, and overcoming. Nietzsche never finished turning it into a clear theory, and much of what he wrote about it was found only in his notebooks after his death. Another strange and powerful idea is the "eternal recurrence", sometimes called the eternal return. Recurrence means happening over and over. Nietzsche introduces the idea in The Gay Science (section 341) as a kind of test. Nietzsche asks the reader to imagine a strange visit. One night a demon comes and speaks. He says that this same life will have to be lived again. Every joy and every pain will return. Every moment, large and small, will come back in the same order, again and again, forever, with nothing new added. How would a person take such news? For some, it would be a heavy burden, almost too much to bear. But a person who truly loved life might welcome it, and even wish for it. Nietzsche uses this thought as a way to measure a life. A person who truly loved their life would be able to face the demon with joy. Some scholars also ask whether Nietzsche believed the eternal return was literally true about the universe. But its main force in his work is as a test of the heart: can a person say "yes" so fully to life that they would happily live it over forever? In Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Nietzsche presents the Übermensch. The word is often translated as "superman", but "overman" or "overhuman" fits better, because it points to the idea of going beyond and overcoming. Zarathustra gives a famous image for it. The human being, he says, is like a rope stretched over a deep gorge, tied between the animal and the overman. To cross such a rope is dangerous, but it is also the great task. The overman is the person who can live without the old God and the old values, and who creates new values out of strength and love of life. Such a person overcomes themselves again and again, instead of standing still. They do not look away from this world toward another, and they do not deny life. For this reason, Nietzsche says, the overman might even look frightening to other people. It is very important to say what the Übermensch is not. It is not a fixed new kind of human, a final stage of evolution, or a master race. It is an ideal of constant self-overcoming, always reaching beyond what a person already is. Reading it as a kind of super-race is a serious mistake, and that mistake later did real harm, as the next section explains. Behind many of these ideas lies one feeling that Nietzsche prized above all. He called it by the Latin phrase amor fati, which means "love of fate". To have amor fati is to love everything that happens in one's life, the bad as well as the good, and to wish for nothing to be different. This connects the will to power, the eternal return, and the overman into a single attitude. The eternal return tests whether a person can love their fate that much. The overman can be understood as a figure of this kind of strength that says yes to life. For Nietzsche, the highest goal was not to escape suffering or to reach a calm heaven, but to say a deep and joyful "yes" to life exactly as it is. His famous line "What does not kill me makes me stronger", from Twilight of the Idols, belongs to this same spirit. Nietzsche also had bold ideas about truth and knowledge. He doubted that anyone could see the world without having a point of view. He argued that all seeing and all knowing come from some particular position, with its own interests and limits. This idea is often called "perspectivism", from the word "perspective", meaning a point of view. This does not quite mean that "anything goes" or that every opinion is as good as every other. Nietzsche's point was that taking in more points of view gives a fuller and fairer understanding. There is no view from outside the world, but some points of view see more than others. This part of his work later became very important for thinkers who study how knowledge and power are linked. Nietzsche wrote many books. Some of the most important are: A book called The Will to Power is sometimes listed among his works, but Nietzsche never wrote it as a finished book. It was put together after his death from his private notebooks. The next section explains why this matters. The story of how Nietzsche was read after his death is almost as strange as his ideas. During his years of illness, and after his death, his sister, Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche, took more and more control of his writings. She outlived him by many years and ran an archive devoted to his work. She also edited his unpublished notes, and from them she helped to shape the book called The Will to Power. Elisabeth had been married to a man named Bernhard Förster, who hated Jews and dreamed of a "pure" German colony. Nietzsche himself had disliked his brother-in-law's views and had spoken against the hatred of Jews. Yet over time his sister steered his name closer to German nationalism. Years later, the Nazi Party and its leader Adolf Hitler treated Nietzsche as one of their heroes. They lifted single lines and words out of his books and used them to support ideas about race, war, and the rule of the strong. Scholars now agree that this picture was false. Nietzsche was not a Nazi, and he was not even an early model for the Nazis. That description fits his brother-in-law far better, and Nietzsche had opposed those very views. The Nazis took his claims out of their setting and bent them to serve their own needs. After the Second World War, writers such as Walter Kaufmann worked to clear his name and to show the real shape of his thought. The truth, however, is not simple, and it is fair to readers to say so plainly. Nietzsche was not a Nazi, but he was also not a comfortable, modern liberal. He wrote harsh things about equality, about democracy, and about whole groups of people, and he defended rank and hardness. It is also too simple to put all the blame on his sister, as if she alone had spoiled a gentle thinker. The honest position lies in between. His own views were often hard and troubling, but the Nazi version of Nietzsche was still a distortion of what he himself wrote. Few modern thinkers have had a wider effect than Nietzsche, even though he was almost unknown while he could still work. His influence reaches across the whole of the twentieth century and beyond. He is often seen as a father of existentialism, a movement that asks how people can make meaning in a world without a fixed plan. Several major philosophers wrote long studies of his work. They include Martin Heidegger, Michel Foucault, Gilles Deleuze, and Jacques Derrida. The French thinkers among them read him above all as a doubter of fixed truth. Nietzsche is also often linked to the new study of the mind. Many readers have compared him with Sigmund Freud, the founder of psychoanalysis, because both wrote about hidden drives in the mind. Freud knew of Nietzsche's importance, but he did not simply present himself as Nietzsche's follower. His influence also runs through literature and the arts. Writers, poets, composers, and painters have all drawn on his images and his daring. Because his work can be read in so many ways, many different groups have tried to claim him as their own. That very richness is part of why people still read and argue about Friedrich Nietzsche.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau, (28 June 1712 – 2 July 1778) was a famous French-speaking philosopher. He was born in Geneva, Switzerland and always described himself as being Genevan. Rousseau lived in the 18th century during the Age of Enlightenment. His political ideology influenced the French Revolution and aided the development of nationalism and socialist theories. Rousseau was also a composer, writing numerous books about music theory. Rousseau authored Confessions, an autobiography, one of the first of its kind. Many later philosophers were influenced by him. He wrote a novel Julie, ou la nouvelle Héloïse, which was a best-seller and influenced 19th century writers of romanticism. Rousseau believed that men were born good and innocent, and that corruption and sadness happened because of life experiences and experiences in society. He believed that if society were gone, man would be happy and pure once again. Rousseau is most famous for his social contract ideology, which is often compared to the social contract of John Locke. This ideology is stated in Rousseau's book, The Social Contract.

Arthur Schopenhauer (February 22, 1788 in Danzig – September 21, 1860 in Frankfurt am Main) was a German philosopher. He was influenced by Kant, Plato and eastern teachings, especially Buddhism and the Upanishads. Schopenhauer believed that the primary characteristic, or essence of all things - including human beings - is not intelligence, rationality or spirit, but will. By "will" he means a wanting and craving like that which we know in ourselves as our "will." It is the source of immense amounts of suffering in the world. He also believed that a "better consciousness" could be attained by denying the fulfilment of our desires, taking time to think about who we really are and what we should do to avoid suffering - but also, in doing something few philosophers of his day spoke of: in making and looking at works of art, especially music, which he considered a way to escape from the world's pain and suffering. Schopenhauer was a huge influence on Richard Wagner, Friedrich Nietzsche, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Thomas Mann, Sigmund Freud, Leo Tolstoy, Carl Jung, Emil Cioran and many other important artists and thinkers of the 20th century.

Herbert Spencer (27 April 1820 – 8 December 1903) was an British philosopher, and a prominent liberal political and social theorist of the Victorian era. Spencer developed an all-embracing conception of evolution. He saw evolution as the progressive development of the physical world, biological organisms, the human mind, and human culture and societies. Spencer never married; he remained a bachelor. He contributed to a wide range of subjects, including ethics, religion, politics, philosophy, biology, sociology, and psychology. Like Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace, he read Malthus' Essay on the principle of population, and was deeply impressed by its argument. Malthus said that sooner or later population growth gets checked by famine and disease, and there are then many deaths. So, he was prepared for Darwin's idea of natural selection, which he preferred to call "survival of the fittest". He did this in Principles of Biology (1864), after reading Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species. "This survival of the fittest, which I have here sought to express in mechanical terms, is that which Mr. Darwin has called ‘natural selection’, or the preservation of favoured races in the struggle for life." Spencer's term does strongly suggest natural selection, yet as he extended evolution into realms of sociology and ethics, Spencer made use of Lamarckism rather than natural selection, so it seems he was not a Darwinian after all. Others took up his social ideas, and drew the conclusion that it was useless to try and help the poor, and that competition without limits was the way society should go. Darwin himself did not accept these ideas, but they were quite widespread in the United States at the end of the nineteenth century.

Baruch Spinoza also known as Benedict Spinoza (24 November 1632 in Amsterdam – 21 February 1677 in The Hague) was a Dutch philosopher of Portuguese Jewish origin. He is considered to be one of the great Rationalist philosophers of the 17th century. Other famous rationalists include Gottfried Leibniz and René Descartes. Spinoza's ideas were not cherished by the Jewish community in Amsterdam of the time, and Spinoza was excommunicated in 1656. An important idea in Spinoza's philosophy is that God and Nature (meaning everything that exists) are the same thing. Opposing dualism and free will as a determinist, Spinoza said that the body and the mind (soul) are two of God's infinite attributes. There is no good or evil in Nature, and that these words only have meanings for human beings. For a person, an event that leads to happiness is good, and an event that leads to suffering is bad. Spinoza describes two types of thoughts, or emotions: When a person acts from his own nature, he is said to be Active. The more you understand your actions, the more active you become. Active emotions lead to happiness and an understanding of God, as well as to Freedom. When a person is being influenced by another person, or a thing, he is said to be Passive. The goal of every person is to intellectually love God (that is, understand Nature as much as humanly possible).

Emanuel Swedenborg (;; born Emanuel Swedberg on 29 January 1688; died 29 March 1772) was a Swedish scientist, philosopher, theologian, revelator, and mystic. He is best known for his book on the afterlife, Heaven and Hell (1758). He was the father of mineralogy and physiology of brain. His writings inspired Swedenborgianism.

François-Marie Arouet (also known as Voltaire) was a French philosopher. He was born in 1694 and grew up in Poitou. He died in Paris in 1778. Voltaire did not like France at the time because he thought that it was old fashioned. He also did not like the Church and thought that people should be allowed to believe what they want. However he did not like democracy either and thought that a country needed to be led by a wise and strong king. Voltaire had to live in exile in England for three years from 1726 to 1729 where these ideas were more common. He liked the philosophy of John Locke. Voltaire was also a writer. He wrote many books, poems and plays, some of which are still liked today. A lot of his work was against France and the Church. This meant that he was unpopular at first but became more popular towards the time of the French Revolution. He also studied science and wrote a lot about people and places he knew. His writings later led to the French revolution, which changed France from a Hereditary Monarchy into a Republic. Voltaire believed in a God but did not believe in a God personally involved in people's lives, like the Christian God. This is called Deism.

Theodor W. Adorno (;; born Theodor Ludwig Wiesengrund; 11 September 1903 – 6 August 1969) was a German sociologist, philosopher, composer, and music theorist. He designed the F-scale with other researchers at the University of California. This scale tried to measure "the authoritarian personality". F stands for Fascist. He wrote about this in the 1950 book The Authoritarian Personality. He was a Marxist.

Simone Lucie Ernestine Marie Bertrand de Beauvoir (,;; 9 January 1908 – 14 April 1986) was a French author (writer) and philosopher (person who writes about ways of thinking). She wrote novels (stories in a book), articles about philosophy ways of thinking or ways of living, and politics, biographies (books about other people's lives) and an autobiography (a book about her life). Her best known books are She Came to Stay and The Mandarins. Her best known writing about ideas is The Second Sex, which was written in 1949. It describes the bad experiences of women in European society, and suggests how women's lives can be improved. Her full name was Simone Lucie-Ernestine-Marie-Bertrand de Beauvoir. She was born on January 9, 1908 in Paris. She studied mathematics and ways of thinking at the Institut Catholique. Then she studied literature and languages at the Institut Sainte-Marie. As well, she studied ways of thinking at the Sorbonne, which is at the University of Paris. In 1943, de Beauvoir published She Came to Stay, a story about her lover Jean-Paul Sartre (who was also a writer and a philosopher). Next, she wrote a novel called The Mandarins, which won prize. In 1944 de Beauvoir wrote an article called Pyrrhus et Cinéas, which was about a way of thinking about hard choices that people have to make. In 1949, she wrote Le deuxième sexe. It was translated by Howard Parshley to The Second Sex. It describes the bad experiences of women in European society, and suggests how women's lives can be improved. The book also discussed ways of thinking about hard choices. At the end of World War II, de Beauvoir and Sartre started a newspaper about ways of living called Les Temps Modernes. De Beauvoir was bisexual and had sexual relationships with some of her female students. She died of pneumonia. She is buried next to Sartre at the Cimetière du Montparnasse in Paris. When Things of the Spirit Come First, (1979) Beauvoir, Simone de. Woman: Myth & Reality, in Jacobus, Lee A (ed.) A World of Ideas. Bedford/St. Martins, Boston 2006. 780-795

Henri-Louis Bergson (18 October 1859 - 4 January 1941), was a French philosopher. Bergson convinced many thinkers that the processes of immediate experience and intuition are more significant than abstract rationalism and science for understanding reality. He was born on the Rue Lamartine in Paris, France. His mother, Katherine Levison, was of English and Irish Jewish descent. His father, the pianist Michał Bergson, was of Polish Jewish descent. His early childhood was spent mostly in London after his birth. He learned the English language from his mother. He returned to Paris when he was nine years old, and became a naturalized French citizen. He attended the Lycée Fontanes in Paris from 1868 to 1878. There he was given the 1877 prize for school mathematics, for the solution of a mathematical problem. When he was nineteen, he studied at École Normale Supérieure (ENS). He read many philosophy books, especially Herbert Spencer. He was given the 1927 Nobel Prize in Literature. In 4 January 1941, Bergson died in occupied Paris from bronchitis. 1889: Essai sur les données immédiates de la conscience 1932: Les Deux sources de la morale et de la religion

Sir Isaiah Berlin OM, FBA (6 June 1909 – 5 November 1997) was a British philosopher. He was born in Riga, Latvia, which at the time was a part of the Russian Empire. He was Jewish, and was the first Jew to win the prize of a fellowship at All Souls College, Oxford University. Isaiah Berlin was an important person of the 20th century. People see him as an important thinker of Liberalist ideas. He was made a member of the Order of Merit and was a professor at the University of Oxford. He made a distinction between positive liberty and negative liberty. His most famous work is probably Two Concepts of Liberty (where he introduced this distinction.) He died 5 November 1997.

Albert Camus (7 November 1913 – 4 January 1960) was a French writer and thinker. He wrote novels, plays, essays, and newspaper articles. He also worked in the theatre as a director and an actor. He said that he felt happier among theatre people than among writers. In 1957, he won the Nobel Prize in Literature. He was 43 when the prize was announced and 44 when he received it. Only Rudyard Kipling had received it at a younger age. Camus was born in Algeria, which was then ruled by France. His family was very poor. His father died in World War I when Camus was less than one year old. His mother could not read or write. He grew up in a small flat in a poor working-class area of Algiers. The flat had no running water or electricity. He was able to continue at school because a teacher helped him and because he later received money from the state. His poor childhood and his life in Algeria strongly shaped his later work. Camus is best known for three novels: The Stranger (1942), The Plague (1947), and The Fall (1956). He also wrote two long essays about ideas, The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) and The Rebel (1951), as well as four plays of his own. He often wrote about a problem that he called the absurd. Human beings want life to have a clear meaning, but the world gives them no answer. Camus called this conflict the absurd. He said that people should not kill themselves because life has no clear meaning. They should instead see the truth clearly, continue to live, and refuse false hopes. Later, Camus wrote more about revolt. To revolt means to say "no" to something that is wrong or unjust. He believed that revolt could be good, but that it must have limits. He opposed the death penalty and political murder. He refused to support any political system that treated killing as a normal or necessary way to build a better future. However, he was not a pacifist, and he said this clearly. Many people call Camus an existentialist, but he often said that he was not one. He did not want to belong to any complete system of thought. He gave a similar answer when people called him an atheist. Camus also took part in the French resistance against Nazi Germany. He wrote for the secret newspaper Combat and became one of its editors in 1944. After the war, he wrote against the death penalty, the atomic bomb, and totalitarianism. Totalitarianism is a form of government in which the state tries to control every part of public and private life. The war in Algeria caused Camus great pain. He wanted Arab and Berber Algerians to have full political rights, and he publicly called for an end to the colonial system. However, he did not support full independence for Algeria. He hoped instead for a free and federal Algeria that would remain joined to France. In this system, Muslim Algerians and French settlers would have the same rights. He also refused to accept the killing of civilians by either side. In 1956, he went to Algiers and asked both sides to stop attacking civilians. His plan failed. After this, he said very little in public about Algeria, although he continued to help prisoners in private. Camus died in a car crash in 1960, at the age of 46. In the car was the unfinished manuscript of his novel The First Man. The book was published in 1994, thirty-four years after his death. The earliest known member of the Camus family in Algeria was Claude Camus. He was born in Bordeaux in 1809. He and his wife crossed the Mediterranean Sea soon after France began to rule Algeria. Older books often say that the Camus family came from Alsace. Camus also tells this story in The First Man. However, this was probably only a family story. Olivier Todd, one of Camus's biographers, studied the official records and found evidence that the family came from the Bordeaux region instead. This also makes it more likely that they went to Algeria for economic reasons rather than political ones. French troops landed in Algeria in 1830. The fighting continued for many years, while more and more European settlers arrived. By 1848, there were nearly 100,000 settlers in Algeria. They came not only from France, but also from Spain, Italy, and Malta. By 1936, about one million Europeans lived in Algeria. When the Algerian War began in 1954, Europeans made up about one ninth of the population. The children and grandchildren of these settlers later became known as pieds-noirs, which means "black feet" in French. Nobody knows for certain where this name came from. Some people say that it referred to the colour of the settlers' shoes. Others say that it came from the muddy feet of farm workers. Camus belonged to this European settler population. His father's family came from the Bordeaux region, while his mother's family came from Menorca, a Spanish island. The European settlers were French citizens. Most Muslim Algerians were legally French subjects, but they did not have the same rights as citizens or the same political power. Algeria was ruled as three departments of France rather than as a separate country. However, the people who lived there did not have equal rights. This inequality is important for understanding Camus's life and work. Albert Camus was born on 7 November 1913 on a farm near the small town of Mondovi, which is now called Dréan. The town is in eastern Algeria, near Annaba. His father, Lucien Auguste Camus, worked in the wine cellars of a company called Jules Ricôme. He watched over the pressing of the grapes and the sending of the wine. His mother was Catherine Sintès. Her family had come to Algeria from the Spanish island of Menorca. She was one of nine children in a poor family. Albert had one brother, Lucien, who was three years older. World War I began in 1914, and Lucien Camus was called into the French army. He served with the Zouaves, a French army unit formed in North Africa. He was badly wounded at the Battle of the Marne. He died in a military hospital on 11 October 1914, at the age of 28. Albert was less than one year old and never knew his father. His mother kept only a photograph of him and a piece of the shell that had killed him. Lucien Camus is buried at Saint-Brieuc in Brittany. His wife never saw his grave. Albert first visited it in 1947. There was one story about his father that Camus never forgot. His father once got up early to watch a man being killed in public by guillotine. The man had murdered a whole family, and Lucien Camus thought that the punishment was fair. However, the sight made him ill. He came home without speaking, lay down, and was sick for much of the morning. Camus used this story three times: near the end of The Stranger, in The Plague, and in his essay "Reflections on the Guillotine". He also told it again in The First Man. In that book, the story troubles the boy so deeply that he has the same nightmare for the rest of his life. When her husband was called into the army in August 1914, Catherine Camus had no money of her own. She therefore moved with her two sons into her mother's flat in Belcourt, a poor working-class district of Algiers. The family moved there a few weeks before they learned that Lucien Camus had died. The flat was on the top floor and had three small rooms and a kitchen. There were two other flats on the same floor, and the three families shared one toilet in the hall. Until 1930, the flat had no running water and no electricity. An oil lamp hung above the only table, where the family ate and the children did their school work. Six people lived there: Albert, his brother, his mother, his grandmother, and two uncles. Albert and Lucien shared one bed until Albert was seventeen. During the war, his mother worked in a factory where she sorted bullets. Later, she cleaned houses and washed clothes for other people. Catherine Camus could not read or write. She was partly deaf and had difficulty speaking. She said some words wrongly and used very few words. Because of this, she was shy with people she did not know and spoke very little at home. Writers do not agree about the cause of these problems. One family story says that she spoke easily when she was young, but that her speech changed in 1914 when she learned that her husband was dead. Another account says that an illness during childhood left her deaf and made her difficult to understand. She had lived in a village where there was no doctor. Camus loved his mother deeply throughout his life, but they almost never talked. He wrote many times about the silence between them. In The First Man, the main character asks his mother about his dead father but learns almost nothing. The book gives one reason for this silence: poor people have fewer things to remember because their days are much the same and they rarely leave the place where they live. The head of the family was Camus's grandmother, who was also called Catherine. She was a hard, proud, and bitter woman who had also lost her husband when she was young. She took the place of her daughter as the person who raised the two boys. She beat them with a whip made from the dried neck of a bull. Their mother stood nearby and only asked the grandmother not to hit them on the head. Another adult in the flat was Camus's uncle Étienne, who made wooden barrels. He could not speak at all until he was a teenager. After an operation, he learned to speak, but he spoke slowly and used only simple words. He also communicated through sounds and signs. He had a dog and a hunting gun, and he cleaned both of them on the family table. Camus loved him and later placed characters based on him in several of his books. Camus wrote about his childhood many times, but he gave two different pictures of it. In some writings, he showed it as very hard. In others, he remembered it as happy. In 1958, a new edition of his first book was published, and Camus wrote a new preface for it. In this preface, he said that poverty had never been a complete misfortune for him because the light of Algeria had always balanced it. He explained that poverty stopped him from believing that everything in the world was good, while the sun taught him that history was not the only important thing. The family lived in real poverty, but Camus still remembered Belcourt with pleasure. The district had a beach, a library, cinemas, and cafés. French, Spanish, Italian, Maltese, and Jewish people lived there. Camus swam, played in the street, and walked around the town with his friends. The difference between the dark rooms of the family flat and the bright sea remained important in all his writing. He often placed these two images next to each other. Camus began attending the boys' school in Belcourt in 1918. He was a very good pupil and was especially good at reading and writing. His teacher was Louis Germain. Germain saw that the boy was clever, but Camus's grandmother wanted him to leave school and begin earning money. Germain argued with the family and persuaded them to let Albert continue. He then taught Albert and two other boys every day after school so that they could take the examination for a scholarship. Because his father had died in the war, Albert was also a pupille de la nation, or "child of the nation". He and his brother received this official position in May 1920. The French state gave children in this position a small amount of money each year to pay for school materials. Camus won a scholarship and entered the Grand Lycée, the large secondary school in Algiers, in October 1924. Some older books say that he entered it in 1923. His time at the school was interrupted at the end of 1930, when doctors found tuberculosis in his lungs. He later returned, repeated his final year, and completed his secondary studies in 1932. Camus never forgot Louis Germain and always said that the teacher had changed his life. He described Germain as strict but kind. Many years later, after receiving the Nobel Prize, Camus wrote to him and thanked him. Sport was more important to the young Camus than school work. Most of the friends he made before 1930 were friends from sport. He played football, usually as a goalkeeper but sometimes as a forward. He first played for a small club called Association Sportive Montpensier. Around 1928, he joined the junior team of Racing Universitaire Algérois, usually called RUA. This was the sports club of the students of Algiers. Camus was small for his age, but he threw himself at the feet of other players to stop the ball and was often hurt. Many years later, he wrote about football in a magazine for former members of the club. He said that much of what he knew about right and wrong had been learned through sport. A friend once asked him whether he would have chosen football or the theatre if his health had allowed him to choose freely. Camus immediately answered that he would have chosen football. During the winter of 1930, Camus began to cough blood. He was taken to the Mustapha Hospital in Algiers, where doctors found tuberculosis in his right lung. Tuberculosis is a serious disease that often attacks the lungs. Camus had just turned seventeen. At that time, there was no medicine that could cure the disease. Doctors used a treatment called artificial pneumothorax. They pushed air into the space around the lung so that the lung became flat and the sick part could rest. The treatment had to be repeated, often every two weeks. Camus had to return for this treatment many times during his life. In 1942, tuberculosis also attacked his other lung. Some of his friends thought that a football match played in heavy rain had caused the illness. Others said that it began after a ball hit him in the chest while he was playing in goal. Neither football nor being hit by a ball causes tuberculosis. However, hard exercise, poor housing, and too little food can make the disease worse. Tuberculosis changed the whole course of Camus's life. He had to stop playing football in serious competitions. Hard exercise remained dangerous for him, although he continued to swim for many years. The illness later stopped him from becoming a university teacher. It also kept him out of the army during World War II, although he asked to join in 1939. Camus later said something surprising about his illness. He said that it had made him free. Because he knew that he might die young, he felt free to choose the kind of life he wanted to live. After becoming ill, Camus went to live with his aunt Antoinette and her husband, Gustave Acault. Acault was a butcher, and the couple had no children. Life in their home was much easier than life in Belcourt. Camus had a room of his own and ate red meat every day because doctors at the time believed that meat helped people with tuberculosis. Acault was also a serious reader and was known for his free-thinking ideas. He gave his nephew books, including Les Nourritures terrestres by André Gide. Many years later, Camus said that Acault had been a kind of father to him. In October 1930, Camus entered the philosophy class at his school. His new teacher was Jean Grenier, who was 32 years old and had recently arrived in Algeria. Grenier noticed that his best pupil was missing. When he learned that Camus was ill, he took a taxi across Algiers to visit him in the flat in Belcourt. The visit was difficult. Camus said very little, and both the teacher and the pupil felt uncomfortable because of the poverty of the rooms. Ten years later, Camus wrote to Grenier about that visit. He explained that his silence had not meant that he was unfriendly. He also said that Grenier's visit had made him feel that he was not as poor as he had believed. Grenier became the most important teacher in Camus's life. For the next thirty years, he read and judged almost everything that Camus wrote. His comments were often very severe. Camus dedicated two of his early books to him. His illness caused him to lose one year of school. In the spring of 1932, he was still writing essays for Grenier's philosophy class. He entered the khâgne only in October of that year. The khâgne was a special class in Algiers for pupils who hoped to enter the famous higher schools in Paris. Camus then entered the University of Algiers. At first he studied literature, but one year later he changed to philosophy. He had wanted to try to enter the École Normale Supérieure in Paris, one of the most famous schools in France, but he gave up the plan. The second year of preparation that he needed was not offered in Algeria. He also could not pay to live in Paris, and his poor health made the plan even more difficult. Camus always had to work while he was studying. During the summer, he worked in a food shop and in his uncle's butcher shop. He also taught younger pupils, sold car parts, worked as a clerk in a shipping office, and worked in the Algiers city office that gave licences for cars. He hated this last job and later used his experience of office work in The Stranger. After finishing his studies, he also worked at the Institute of Meteorology in Algiers from November 1937 until September 1938. In 1936, Camus completed his final university paper. It was about Christian thought and Neoplatonism, a later school of Greek philosophy. The paper compared Plotinus, a Greek thinker, with Augustine of Hippo, a Christian writer from North Africa. It earned Camus the diplôme d'études supérieures, an advanced university degree. His illness then stopped him from continuing towards a teaching career. A new attack of tuberculosis in 1937 meant that he was not allowed to take the agrégation, the state examination needed to become a university teacher. On 16 June 1934, Camus married Simone Hié. He was twenty years old. Hié was the daughter of a doctor in Algiers and was well known in the small social world of the city. People talked about her clothes and her love affairs. Such behaviour shocked many people in Algiers during the 1930s. She had earlier planned to marry one of Camus's friends, Max-Pol Fouchet. After she married Camus, the two young men never spoke to each other again. In practice, the marriage lasted little more than one year. The couple separated in 1936, but their divorce was not completed until 1940. For a time after the separation, Camus lived with three other students in a house above the bay of Algiers. They called it "the house facing the world". Camus later remembered those months as an unexpected period of happiness in a difficult life. Camus first joined a political group in 1933. It was an anti-fascist movement started by the writers Henri Barbusse and Romain Rolland. Two years later, he joined the French Communist Party. Most writers now say that he joined in 1935, although some older books give the end of 1934. Camus did not join because he believed in Marxism. He later said that he had never read Marx or Engels before joining the party. He told Jean Grenier that he had to become a Communist because he wanted to remain close to the poor people from whom he came. For Camus, joining the party in 1935 meant standing beside writers such as André Gide and André Malraux. It did not mean supporting Stalin or the leaders of the party, who meant little to him. His main work for the party was to bring Arab and Berber people into it. He later said that this work made up about half of everything he did for the party. It was also the first time that he truly met Muslim people who had received the same kind of education as himself. French and Muslim children in colonial Algeria did not normally meet at school or while playing. Camus was never an important party leader and never held a high position. However, he was probably the best-known Communist in the cultural life of Algeria. At first, the Communists in Algeria belonged to the French Communist Party. In 1936, they became a separate Algerian Communist Party. This was the party that later expelled Camus. The Communist Party then changed its political position. Joseph Stalin wanted France to become an ally against Nazi Germany. The Soviet Union therefore told Communist parties in other countries to support the French government. In Algeria, this caused a major change. The Communists had worked with the Algerian nationalist leader Messali Hadj, but they now turned against him, and his movement was banned. Camus refused to accept this change and would not break with the Algerian nationalists. He continued to ask for rights for the Algerian people after the party had ended that campaign. Because of this, he was judged by members of the party and then expelled. Even the local leader Amar Ouzegane, who liked Camus, could not protect him. Writers give slightly different dates for the break. A recent study of all the evidence places it in the autumn of 1937, while an older biography gives November 1937. Camus never joined another political party. He once joked that the only party he could join would be a party of people who were not certain that they were right. In 1936, Camus and a group of young actors created a theatre company called the Théâtre du Travail, which means "Workers' Theatre". Its money came from the Communist House of Culture in Algiers. Their first play was Le Temps du mépris, which was based on a novel by André Malraux. Camus directed the play and also acted in it. Their next work was Révolte dans les Asturies ("Revolt in Asturias"), which Camus and his friends wrote together. It was about a workers' revolt in Spain. The city government of Algiers banned the play before the group could perform it. The House of Culture closed in 1937, and the Théâtre du Travail ended with it. In October 1937, Camus created a new company of his own, the Théâtre de l'Équipe, or "Team Theatre". In the same year, he also directed Prometheus Bound by Aeschylus. This Greek play is about a hero who is punished for helping human beings and refuses to say that he was wrong. Camus loved the theatre throughout his life. He said that he felt happy and relaxed among theatre people, but uncomfortable among writers and thinkers. Camus published his first book in Algiers in 1937. It was called L'Envers et l'endroit. Its English titles include The Wrong Side and the Right Side and Betwixt and Between. The book contains five essays about his childhood, old age, and death. He wrote them in 1935 and 1936 and dedicated the book to Jean Grenier. Only a small number of copies were printed, and the book was not published again until 1958. One of Camus's friends told him that he used the word "I" too often. Camus agreed and said that a writer should remain behind the scenes. His second book was Noces ("Nuptials"), which was printed in Algiers in May 1939. Some books give 1938 instead. It contains four essays about the sun, the sea, and the ruins of Tipasa. Like his first book, it received almost no attention in France. The essay "Nuptials at Tipasa" is the best known of the four. In it, Camus describes a day among Roman ruins beside the sea. He writes that everything there seemed unimportant except the sun, kisses, and the wild smells of the earth. Camus called such moments bonheur, the French word for happiness. For him, this meant short moments in which a person feels completely joined to nature. He believed that such moments should not last too long. At about the same time, Camus began writing his first novel, La Mort heureuse ("A Happy Death"). He did not publish it. It appeared in 1971, many years after his death. In September 1938, Pascal Pia employed Camus as an editorial secretary for a new newspaper called Alger républicain. Pia had been sent from Paris to create the paper. It was published from 6 October 1938 until 28 October 1939. The newspaper said that it spoke for all the people of Algeria, including both Muslims and French settlers. It opposed hatred of Jewish people and the laws that placed Muslim Algerians in a lower position. Camus was not yet twenty-five. Pia employed many young and inexperienced writers because he did not have enough money to pay older journalists. Camus reported on the courts and watched many trials. He later used this experience in The Stranger. He also wrote about a prison ship carrying 609 men. He described its very small cages and lack of light, and wrote that he was ashamed to be there. In July 1939, the police broke up a public meeting held by Algerian nationalists. Camus then wrote a short article called "Unfortunate Arrests" and asked for the arrested men to be freed. Publicly defending Algerian nationalists was unusual and dangerous in colonial Algeria in 1939. Camus published articles under his own name, but he also used several false names. One of them was "Jean Meursault", a name that he later used again for the main character of The Stranger. He also wrote reviews of books. On 20 October 1938, he reviewed La Nausée ("Nausea") by Jean-Paul Sartre. He recognised in the novel an idea close to his own idea of the absurd. However, he thought that the book was too abstract and that Sartre did not make good use of the freedom he gave to his characters. In June 1939, Camus wrote a group of eleven articles about Kabylia, a mountain region of Algeria where many Berber people live. Together, the articles are known as "The Misery of Kabylia". Each article was printed with at least one photograph. Camus travelled to the villages himself. He wrote about poor housing, the lack of clean water, and the small number of doctors. He also gave figures about schools, population, and the age at which people died. He showed that the land was much too crowded. About 247 people lived on each square kilometre, compared with 71 in France. The people ate wheat, whose price had increased, but they grew olives and figs, whose prices had not increased. Many people lived on gifts from others or ate herbs, roots, and thistles because they did not have enough food. In one village, a man showed Camus his young daughter. She was very thin and wore torn clothes. The man asked whether she would not be as beautiful as a French girl if he could give her enough food and better clothes. Camus wrote that he could never forget this meeting. The articles angered the French rulers of Algeria. The governor of Algeria visited Kabylia soon afterwards, although it is difficult to know how much Camus's articles caused the visit. Camus's widow later said that the authorities had tried to pay him to remain silent before the articles were published. Readers have understood the articles in different ways. Many European readers described them as anti-colonial writing, and the Tunisian writer Albert Memmi called them honest and humane. One recent writer believes that this judgement is too generous. He argues that Camus wanted better living conditions for the Kabyle people, but still expected them to remain under French rule. From this point of view, Camus wanted to reform colonialism, not bring it to an end. By 1939, Alger républicain was in serious trouble. Camus and Pia had written against the coming war. When the war began, the government placed censors inside the newspaper office. The censors removed whole articles, and empty spaces appeared on the printed pages because Camus refused to replace the missing words with patriotic writing. He signed some articles with false names and printed passages by older French writers instead. On one occasion, he challenged the censors to remove a passage written by Montaigne. Alger républicain published its final issue on 28 October 1939. Pia and Camus had also started an evening newspaper called Le Soir républicain in September 1939. It continued for a few more months under Camus's direction, but the authorities closed it on 10 January 1940. The owners said that Camus had turned the paper into a personal political campaign. Camus wrote to Jean Grenier that this was true. He said that he had used the newspaper to defend freedom of thought against the censors and to oppose the war without hating anyone. Camus was now without a job and had little hope of finding another one in Algeria because the French colonial authorities did not want him to work there. Foley describes this as a kind of forced exile because the authorities had made it very difficult for Camus to find work in his own country. Pascal Pia found Camus a job in France. Camus arrived in Paris in March 1940 and began working for a large popular newspaper called Paris-Soir. He was an editorial secretary and helped to prepare the pages for printing. He never wrote an article for the paper and did not enjoy the work, but he learned how a large newspaper was produced. The German army attacked France in May 1940. Paris fell in the middle of June, and the newspaper moved south, first to Clermont-Ferrand and then to Lyon. France was divided into two parts. Germany controlled the north and west, while a French government based in Vichy ruled the south. This period is known as Vichy France. On 3 December 1940, Camus married for the second time. His wife was Francine Faure, a mathematics teacher from Oran in Algeria. The wedding was very simple. Pascal Pia and a few people from the newspaper were the only guests. Less than one month later, Camus lost his job because the newspaper had to reduce its staff. Albert and Francine returned to Algeria in January 1941 and lived in Oran. Both of them worked as teachers. Camus did not like the town. He later described it as a town without a soul and as a place that turned its back on the sea. He stayed there for about a year and a half. He could not find regular work, and his health became worse. He taught at a private school for Jewish pupils run by his friend André Bénichou. The children had been removed from state schools because of the laws of the Vichy government. In February 1941, while living in Oran, Camus completed The Myth of Sisyphus. In May 1942, the Paris publisher Gallimard published L'Étranger. The book is known in English as either The Stranger or The Outsider. Later in the same year, Gallimard published Le Mythe de Sisyphe ("The Myth of Sisyphus"). Both books were published in Paris while the city was under German rule. The Stranger appeared in May, when Camus was still living in Algeria. By the time The Myth of Sisyphus was published, he was ill and staying at Le Panelier in the mountains of France. The two books made Camus famous very quickly, and they remain his best-known works. Much of the early success of The Stranger came from a long essay by Jean-Paul Sartre called "Explication de L'Étranger". It was published in the magazine Cahiers du Sud in February 1943. Sartre praised the novel and its plain style, but he was not sure that Camus had fully understood the German and Danish thinkers whose ideas he used. The Stranger is told by a man named Meursault, who works as a clerk in Algiers. The book begins with the death of his mother. Meursault travels to the home for old people where she has lived for several years. He sits beside her body during the night, as people expect him to do. However, he smokes a cigarette, drinks coffee, and falls asleep for a short time. He does not ask to see her face for the last time. He does not know her exact age, and he does not cry. The next day, he goes swimming and meets Marie Cardona, a young woman from his office. He takes her to see a comic film and spends the night with her. After this, his life continues as before. Marie asks whether he loves her. He answers that the word does not mean anything to him, but says that he will marry her if she wants. A neighbour named Raymond Sintès, who is said to make money from women, asks Meursault to write a letter to his Arab mistress. Later, Raymond also asks him to speak for him at the police station. Meursault agrees because agreeing costs him nothing. Meursault, Marie, and Raymond visit a friend's hut beside the sea. A group of Arab men follows them. There is a short fight, and Raymond is cut with a knife. Later, Meursault walks alone in the strong midday sun and meets one of the men again. He shoots him once and then fires four more bullets into his body. During the trial, the court says very little about the killing itself. Instead, it speaks mainly about the funeral. Witnesses say that Meursault did not want to see his mother's body, that he smoked, slept, and drank coffee beside it, that he did not cry, and that he did not know her age. The prosecutor calls Meursault a monster with an empty heart and asks for him to be put to death. He says almost nothing about the man who was killed on the beach. Meursault's own lawyer uses the same kind of argument and asks him to say things that are not true. Meursault refuses. He is sentenced to death. The same ideas return throughout the book: everything is the same to him, nothing is his fault, and nothing matters. At the end, while waiting in his prison cell, he refuses to speak with a priest. He then finds a kind of peace in the thought that the world is as uncaring about him as he is about it. The Arab man whom Meursault kills is never given a name. Later writers have paid much attention to this fact. Readers also warn against a common mistake: Meursault should not simply be understood as Camus speaking for himself. Scholars still disagree about how close the character is to his author. The novel has been understood in many different ways. Some read it as a story about the absurd. Others see Meursault as a man who refuses the lies of society. Some understand the novel mainly through the colonial world of Algeria, while others see it as a trap that tests the reader's own judgement. Camus said that he had three real people in mind when he created Meursault and that he himself was one of the three. In August 1942, Camus went to a small place called Le Panelier in the mountains of the Haute-Loire. His doctor had advised him to breathe mountain air. Le Panelier is near the village of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon. During the war, many people in Le Chambon and the villages around it worked together to hide Jewish refugees. Yad Vashem in Israel gave the title Righteous Among the Nations to about forty people from the village. It also honoured the rescue work of the community as a whole. Francine returned to Algeria, and Camus planned to join her in November. However, the war changed everything. American forces landed in North Africa in November 1942. The German army then occupied the south of France, and all travel and communication between France and Algeria were cut. Camus could not leave France. He and Francine remained apart until she arrived in Paris in the autumn of 1944, almost two years later. This forced separation later became part of The Plague, in which a whole town is closed and families are separated from one another. In 1943, Pascal Pia was working for the secret resistance newspaper Combat. He asked Camus to join him. Camus moved to Paris near the end of the year. He prepared pages, corrected and edited articles, and wrote articles of his own. For safety, he did not sign them. The articles he wrote in 1944 attacked the German army and secret police. They also attacked Marshal Pétain and the Vichy government. They warned French people who helped the Germans that they would be judged after the war. The work was dangerous. Several members of Combat were arrested, sent to prison camps, or killed. One of them was the poet René Leynaud, a friend of Camus who was shot by the Germans in 1944. Writers give different dates for the time when Camus became the head of the newspaper. Some say that Pia made him editor of the secret paper in 1943. Others say that Pia left in June 1944 to do other resistance work and that Camus took his place at that time. In 1943, Camus also began working for the publisher Gallimard. He remained there until his death. He read new books for the company and directed a series of books of his own. Camus wrote four short essays called "Letters to a German Friend". They are not true letters. They are written as speeches to a German who never answers, and the German is not a real person. Camus wrote the first essay in July 1943, and it appeared in the secret magazine Revue Libre. The second was signed with the false name Louis Neuville and published in Cahiers de la Libération. The third appeared in 1945 in Libertés. The fourth was not published separately. It appeared when all four essays were published together as a book in 1945. Camus dedicated the book to René Leynaud. In these essays, Camus explains why France was slow to fight against Germany. He says that the French needed moral reasons for fighting and could not depend only on love of country. In the final essay, he makes an important argument. He and his German friend began with the same belief: that the world has no meaning. However, they followed different paths. The German chose war and conquest. Camus chose justice. He wrote that although the world itself has no meaning, one thing within it does have meaning: the human being. Human beings matter because they are the only beings who ask for meaning. This is the point at which Camus's idea of the absurd begins to become an idea about how human beings should treat one another. Paris was freed in August 1944. Combat could now be published openly. Camus wrote its leading articles, with titles such as "The Blood of Freedom" and "The Night of Truth". On 21 August, the newspaper welcomed the freeing of the city with an article by Camus called "From Resistance to Revolution". About 200,000 copies were printed. For a time, Combat was seen as the voice of the French Resistance. Many of its readers were young teachers, students, and members of trade unions. Camus became a well-known public figure almost at once. He also used the newspaper to explain what he thought journalism should be. He wrote that newspapers should be free from the control of money. He said that it was better to report true news second than to report false news first. A newspaper should help its readers to understand events clearly instead of only trying to please them. Camus asked Jean-Paul Sartre to write for Combat. Sartre reported on the street fighting during the liberation of Paris. In 1945, Camus sent him to the United States as the newspaper's correspondent. Camus remained at Combat until 1947. He left after arguments inside the newspaper and financial problems that would have forced it to give up its independence. After the war, France had to judge the people who had helped the German forces. This period is called the épuration, or purge. At first, Camus supported severe punishment. He wrote that a country that failed to remove guilty people from public life would also fail to rebuild itself. The Catholic writer François Mauriac disagreed with him and asked for mercy. In January 1945, the writer Robert Brasillach, who had supported Germany, was sentenced to death. Camus was asked to sign a request to Charles de Gaulle to save Brasillach's life. Camus signed the request and explained his reason in a letter. He said that he had always been deeply against the death penalty and that the least he could do was refuse to take part in it. He also said that he had no respect for Brasillach, either as a writer or as a man. The request failed, and Brasillach was shot. Camus soon understood that the purge was not fair. Some people were punished severely, while many others who were also guilty were never judged. In 1948, Camus said publicly that Mauriac had been right. His articles from the war are still difficult to judge because he asked for quick and strong justice even though he opposed the death penalty throughout his life. He later said that the purge had taught him an important lesson: justice that tries to become complete and perfectly pure stops being justice. On 6 August 1945, an American aircraft dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima in Japan. About 80,000 people died at once. Most French newspapers welcomed the event and described it as a great victory. Camus wrote against the bombing on 8 August. He said that a civilisation built on machines had reached its highest point of savagery. He warned that human beings would soon have to choose between destroying themselves together and using science in a wise way. Almost no one in France agreed with him publicly. Only a few writers, including François Mauriac, expressed a similar view. Camus's family life also changed during these months. Francine Camus arrived in Paris from Algeria in October 1944.
