On 5 September 1945, she gave birth to twins, Catherine and Jean. On 25 March 1946, Camus arrived in New York harbour on a ship carrying goods called the Oregon. He was 32 years old. The border officers kept him for a long time, and the French cultural service had to help him enter the country. American security services had collected information about him. They knew that he had once belonged to the Communist Party and that he had worked in the Resistance. On the evening of 28 March, he gave a talk at Columbia University. Every seat was taken, and many people could not enter. No talk in French had ever brought such a large crowd to the university. Camus called his talk "The Human Crisis", and it lasted less than half an hour. He began with four short stories from the war. In one of them, a woman cleans the stairs of a building while two men are being tortured inside. She says that she never becomes involved in the private business of the people who live there. Camus's point was simple: the war had ended, but the sickness that had caused it had not. People had learned to watch murder without feeling horror. He then described the main signs of the crisis. Terror was growing, people no longer tried to persuade one another, leaders understood only victory and defeat, and murder had become accepted. At the end, he asked people to act. He called for clear language, pity for others, small groups of people working together across national borders, and an end to the death penalty everywhere in the world. Few people understood the importance of the talk at the time, but it became better known many years later. In November 1946, Camus wrote a group of eight articles for Combat called "Neither Victims nor Executioners". In these articles, he said that terror had taken control of the world. He gave several reasons for this. People no longer tried to persuade one another, everyone lived among machines and political ideas, and everyone was certain that they were right. The articles asked people to refuse to kill for a political cause. They also asked them to refuse a world in which killing had become normal. Camus returned to these words during the Algerian War. He then said that everyone in Algeria was becoming either a victim or a killer, and sometimes both at the same time. La Peste ("The Plague") was published on 10 June 1947. It won a French prize given by book critics and sold 22,000 copies in two weeks. Camus had worked on the novel for several years. He had thought about calling it The Prisoners or The Separated. Even shortly before it was published, he believed that the book was a failure. The story takes place in Oran during the 1940s. Rats begin to die in the streets. People then begin to die, and the town is closed off from the rest of the world. The main character is Doctor Bernard Rieux. His wife is ill and is staying far away in a hospital in the mountains. His quiet mother lives with him. Several other characters are important. Tarrou is a visitor who lives in a hotel and hates death sentences. Rambert is a newspaper writer who tries to escape from the town. Father Paneloux is a Christian priest. Grand is an office worker who is writing a book but cannot get past its first sentence. Cottard is a man who is pleased that the plague has come. So many people die that the town has to bury large numbers of bodies at the same time. The football stadium becomes a camp where people who may have caught the disease are kept away from everyone else. At the centre of the story is the slow death of a young boy, the son of Judge Othon. Rieux, Tarrou, and the priest watch him die but cannot save him. Love and friendship become difficult because they depend on a future, while the people of Oran have only the present. The novel begins with words from Daniel Defoe. They say that it is reasonable to show one kind of prison by using another, just as it is reasonable to show something real by using something that does not exist. The novel can be understood in several ways. It can be read as a picture of the German occupation of France and the Resistance, as a picture of any great evil, or as a call to fight against a world that has no clear meaning. Camus said that the enemy in the book was never named, although everyone understood who it was. The critic Roland Barthes said that the novel had moved too far away from real history. Camus answered that the plague could stand for any kind of tyranny. He also suggested that this was the very reason why some critics disliked the book. Camus said that the novel marked an important change in his work. The Stranger was about one man alone, while The Plague was about a group of people who shared the same struggle. The book made Camus a best-selling writer. The novel has also been criticised. One criticism was already made while Camus was alive. A disease has no will, and nobody is morally guilty of causing it. For this reason, some readers thought that a plague was a poor picture of a military occupation. The difficult moral choices of the war disappear from the story, as does the fact that people chose to do evil. A second criticism became common around 1970. Almost no Arab people appear in this story about an Algerian city. Only their empty streets are described. Conor Cruise O'Brien wrote that Camus had to remove the Arabs because a story about people living under occupation could not work if the French characters were themselves the occupiers. He called this silence an artistic way of making the Arabs of Oran disappear. Other writers answer that a fable is not meant to be a complete picture of real life. They also point out that Camus was writing openly against colonial violence at the same time. In an article for Combat in May 1947, he wrote that the French were now doing in Algeria what they had blamed the Germans for doing in Europe. In 1951, the Algerian writer Mouloud Feraoun told Camus that he was sorry not to find Algerians in the novel. Camus answered that including them would have meant writing a different book, one about the problem that poisoned every life in Algeria. Camus wrote four plays of his own. Caligula is about a Roman emperor who learns that people die and that the world does not care. He then uses his power to show everyone how mad and cruel the world is. Camus wrote the play in 1938 for his theatre company in Algiers and published its final form in 1944. It was first performed in Paris in September 1945 and was successful. Le Malentendu ("The Misunderstanding" or "Cross Purpose") was written in 1942 and 1943. It is about a man who returns home after many years. His mother and sister do not know who he is, and they kill him for his money. The play was first performed in Paris in 1944, but the public did not receive it warmly. L'État de siège ("State of Siege") appeared in 1948. It is also about a plague, but it does not tell the same story as the novel. In this play, the plague is a person and acts like a dictator. Camus created the work with the actor and director Jean-Louis Barrault. The public did not like it, and it was removed from the theatre after seventeen performances. Les Justes ("The Just Assassins") was first performed in December 1949 and published in 1950. It is about a group of Russian revolutionaries in 1905 who plan to kill a grand duke. One man refuses to throw the bomb because children are travelling in the carriage. He kills the grand duke later, is arrested, and is put to death. Another member of the group is willing to kill the children as well. The play is not simply about a hero fighting a villain. It places two ideas about revolutionary violence against each other. One idea still recognises the value of the life that it destroys and accepts death in return. The other accepts no limit at all. Dora, one of the members of the group, says that even destruction can be done in a right way or a wrong way and that there must be limits. In one scene, a character says that they kill in order to build a world in which nobody will kill again. Another quietly asks what will happen if that world never comes. This question is at the heart of the play. Camus also translated and freely changed plays by other writers. In 1953, he worked on La Dévotion à la croix by Calderón de la Barca and Les Esprits by Pierre de Larivey. In 1955, he worked on Un cas intéressant by Dino Buzzati. In 1956 and 1957 came Le Chevalier d'Olmedo by Lope de Vega and Requiem pour une nonne by William Faulkner. In 1959, he produced The Possessed, based on a novel by Dostoyevsky. In June 1949, Camus left Marseille by ship for a journey through South America, where he gave a number of public talks. The journey ended on 31 August. He was still suffering from tuberculosis. After the journey, he had to rest at Cabris, near Grasse in the south of France. He did not return to Paris until March 1950. L'Homme révolté ("The Rebel") was published on 18 October 1951. It is a long essay about revolutions and about killing for an idea. Camus begins with the absurd. If nothing has any meaning, then nothing is forbidden and murder is allowed. Camus refuses this answer. He says that the act of saying "no" is itself a value. His main example is a slave who says, "Enough!" At that moment, the slave says two things at once. He says no to his master, but he also says yes to something within himself that is worth protecting. He understands that other people share the same value. Camus then makes a difference between revolt and revolution. In his argument, revolt accepts limits. Revolution forgets these limits and kills people in the name of a future that never arrives. Most of the book discusses people and political movements that Camus believed had followed the wrong path. These include the Marquis de Sade, the Romantic poets, Hegel, characters created by Dostoyevsky, the Russian revolutionaries of 1905, the Nazis, and the Communists. Camus admired the Russian bomb throwers of 1905 because they accepted death in return for the life they had taken. He compared them with later political movements that killed people without accepting any limits. The final part of the book praises what Camus calls Mediterranean thought. He connects clear thought and moral limits with the light of the Mediterranean Sea. Many readers did not accept this idea. The book made many people angry. Some were angry because Camus placed Nazism and communism beside each other. Others were angry because he did not include colonial rule in his history of revolt. Camus also argued with André Breton, the leader of the surrealist artists, whom he had criticised in the book. Camus and Jean-Paul Sartre met in Paris in 1943, during the German occupation, and quickly became friends. They met in cafés, talked, and drank together. The two men were very different. Sartre had studied at the École Normale Supérieure, while Camus had grown up in poverty in Belcourt. Sartre had received much more formal training in philosophy. In his 1943 essay about The Stranger, he had already written that Camus quoted German thinkers whom he did not always understand. Camus refused a place on the board of Sartre's magazine Les Temps modernes in 1944. The two men also argued in public in 1948 about the meaning of democracy. Their first serious quarrel happened in 1946 at a party given by the writer Boris Vian. The philosopher Maurice Merleau-Ponty argued that everyone had to choose a side in the Cold War and that political violence could sometimes be accepted. Camus shouted at him and left the flat. The final break came after the publication of The Rebel. Nobody at Sartre's magazine Les Temps modernes wanted to review the book. Sartre finally gave the work to Francis Jeanson. He said that Jeanson would be the hardest critic, but would at least be polite. The review appeared in May 1952 and was very severe. Jeanson asked a difficult question. Camus had written about the people who suffered under Stalin, but what about the people who suffered under Western countries and colonial rule? Camus answered in the same magazine in August. He did not write directly to Jeanson. Instead, he wrote to Sartre as the person in charge of the magazine. Camus complained that the review had replaced his real book with a different one. He said that when he wrote that the sky was blue and someone told him that he had written that it was black, either he was mad or the other person could not hear. Sartre's reply appeared in the same issue. It was twenty pages long and even more severe. He laughed at Camus's pride and at his idea of Mediterranean limits. Sartre said that a person who wanted to guide others in a struggle first had to take part in that struggle. In Foley's reading, neither Jeanson nor Sartre answered the question that Camus believed was most important: whether the Marxist view of history leads to tyranny. The two men never spoke again. Most readers at the time believed that Sartre had won the argument, and Camus was left alone. Camus wrote a long answer to all the attacks called "Defence of The Rebel", but it was not published during his lifetime. La Chute ("The Fall") was published in May 1956. It is a short novel written as one long speech. A man called Jean-Baptiste Clamence speaks to a stranger in an Amsterdam bar called the Mexico-City. He was once a successful lawyer in Paris. He now calls himself a judge-penitent, a man who admits his own wrong acts while judging the wrong acts of others. He tells the stranger about a night when a young woman threw herself from a bridge into the River Seine. Clamence was walking past. He heard the sound of her falling into the water and then heard her cries, but he continued walking and did nothing. He has never been able to forget the event. He later explains that the more he accuses himself, the more right he feels he has to judge everyone else. Clamence also keeps a stolen painting in his cupboard. It is a real panel painted by Jan van Eyck. It was stolen from a church in Ghent in 1934 and has never been found. Readers often notice the change in the light and weather of Camus's novels. The Stranger and The Plague take place in the strong sun of North Africa. The Fall takes place among fog, rain, and dark water. Its main subject is guilt, while the earlier books were more concerned with innocence. Many people have read the novel as a book about Camus himself. His wife Francine believed that it was about his love affairs during their marriage. She told him that he owed the book to her. Other readers see it as an answer to Sartre and to the writers who had attacked The Rebel. L'Exil et le Royaume ("Exile and the Kingdom") was published in 1957. It contains six short stories. One of them, "The Adulterous Woman", grew from a journey that Camus made to Laghouat in southern Algeria in December 1952. Camus said that each story dealt with exile in a different way. He explained that the kingdom in the title meant a free and simple life that human beings had to find again. The best-known story is "The Guest". A French teacher living in the mountains of Algeria is ordered to take an Arab prisoner to the police. He does not want to do it. He takes the man halfway, gives him food and money, and then allows him to choose his own road. The prisoner chooses the road leading to the prison. The teacher returns to his classroom and finds a message on the blackboard. It says that he has handed over their brother and that he will be punished for it. Readers disagree about the meaning of the ending. Some see the teacher as a good man caught in a situation from which there is no good way out. Others think it is strange that the only kind person in a story about colonial Algeria is a European settler. In 1957, Camus published a long essay called "Reflections on the Guillotine". It appeared in a book that also contained an essay by Arthur Koestler. The essay begins with the story of Camus's father and the public execution that made him ill. Camus argues that when the killing of a prisoner makes even a decent citizen sick, it cannot be bringing peace to society. He also says that silence about the death penalty helps it to continue. The same is true when people use soft or unclear words to describe it. Camus points out that the same crime might lead to death in one part of France but not in another. He also argues that a court which admits that it can make mistakes should not give a punishment that can never be corrected. He asks France to end the death penalty and replace it with hard labour. He adds that hard labour at least leaves a prisoner the choice of dying. François Mauriac criticised the essay. He said that talking about the death penalty allowed people to avoid more urgent subjects, such as torture in Algeria. Camus opposed the death penalty from his youth until his death. He also acted against it. He personally gave Charles de Gaulle letters asking him to show mercy to prisoners who had been sentenced to death. Camus also spoke in support of people suffering in other countries. On 15 March 1957, he gave a speech at the Salle Wagram in Paris against the actions of the Soviet army in Hungary. He said that Hungary had become what Spain had been twenty years earlier. He argued that a country under totalitarian rule could not slowly become better. Terror, he said, only became worse, and the gallows could never become kind. In 1957, Camus also refused to join a government group created to study abuse and torture in Algeria. He refused because the group had no clear powers and was not free from government control. Algeria is central to understanding Camus. He was born there, his mother lived there throughout her life, and most of his family and friends were there. At the same time, he saw that life in Algeria was deeply unjust. From his first years as a newspaper writer, he wrote about the poverty of Arab and Berber people. He also spoke against colonial violence in other countries. In 1947, for example, he attacked the French killings in Madagascar. In 1943, Camus wrote in his diary that returning to Algeria was like looking at the face of a child. However, he added that he knew that not everything there was innocent or pure. The war in Europe ended on 8 May 1945. On that day, Algerian nationalists marched while carrying their own flag. They wanted both to celebrate the end of the war and to protest against the removal of their leader, Messali Hadj. In several towns, especially Sétif and Guelma, the marches became violent. About one hundred French people were killed, some of them in very cruel ways. The French answer was much larger. For several weeks, the police, the army, and groups of European settlers killed Algerians. French aircraft also bombed villages. Nobody knows the exact number of people who died. The French government gave a figure of about 1,500. A French parliamentary group gave a figure of 15,000, while later Algerian sources gave much higher numbers. Many people see these killings as the true beginning of the Algerian War, nine years before the war officially began. Camus had travelled through Algeria for several weeks in April 1945. He returned to Paris only a few days before the violence began. From 13 to 23 May, he published eight articles in Combat under the title "Crisis in Algeria". Six of these articles were later included in his book of writings about Algeria.

Gilles Deleuze (, "zheel duh-LOOZ"); 18 January 1925 – 4 November 1995) was a French philosopher. He wrote about philosophy, literature, movie, and art. His most popular books were the two parts of Capitalism and Schizophrenia. The first part is titled Anti-Oedipus (1972), and the second part is titled A Thousand Plateaus (1980). Both books were written with his academic partner Félix Guattari. He also wrote Difference and Repetition (1968). Some people think that he is among the greatest philosophers. His work is considered very important in philosophy and art, including literary theory, semiotics, poststructuralism, postmodernism, and psychoanalysis. He has also grown popular in antipsychiatry communities for his criticisms of the psychoanalytic movement, but this remains widely questioned. Deleuze was born in Paris and lived there most of his life. He went to school during World War II and later studied philosophy and history at the University of Paris. He started teaching philosophy in 1948, and taught at several universities. He married Denise Paul "Fanny" Grandjouan in 1956. Deleuze worked at the University of Vincennes in Saint-Denis from 1969 to 1987. There he became friends and worked with Michel Foucault and Félix Guattari, his friendship with Michel Foucault coming to an end in 1977 after a disagreement on the concept of desire as a productive force. He had a lung removed in 1968 because he had tuberculosis. It was difficult for him to breathe for the rest of his life. He died by committing suicide in 1995.

Jacques Derrida (15 July 1930 - 9 October 2004) was a French philosopher. He was born in El Biar, French Algeria into a family of Sephardi Jews. originally from Toledo, Spain. He developed a form of semiotic analysis known as deconstruction. His work is called post-structualism and associated with postmodern philosophy. He died of pancreatic cancer in a Paris hospital.

John Dewey (20 October 1859 - June 1st 1952) was an American psychologist and philosopher. He was born in Burlington, Vermont. Dewey graduated from the University of Vermont. He later taught at many schools. In September 1882, Dewey went to the Johns Hopkins University and studied philosophy and psychology and published the paper, "The New Psychology" in the Andover Review in 1884. Afterwards, he taught psychology at universities and later on, got married to his former student Alice Chipman. In 1886, he started a new school which came to be known as the "Laboratory School" or "Dewey School". This school taught pragmatism, which says that a school's curriculum should be based on everyday life, lessons, and focuses on hands-on activities to better help students learn. His wife Alice was principal of the "Dewey School" from 1901 to 1904. After he retired as a teacher, he continued watching and figuring the society and politics. John Dewey died in 1952. John Dewey believed in the "theory of inquiry", which shows how animals survived in their environment. He used the theory in the way he taught. He said that children learn best with real-life problems and hands-on activities. His most well-known essay was "The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology" (1896) which created the stimulus that became the response, which later became known as social behaviorism. For example, a person focuses on something, decides what to do, then acts on the decision.

Ralph Waldo Emerson (May 25, 1803 – April 27, 1882) was an American author, poet, and philosopher. Emerson was born in Boston, Massachusetts in 1803. His father was a Unitarian minister. He chose not to follow the beliefs of the Unitarians and instead, created his own world view, Transcendentalism. He first wrote about this view in an essay called Nature in 1836. Emerson's father died when he was only eight years old. He studied at school in Boston and went to Harvard University, one of the most well-rated universities in the country. Many men were heads of a town church in Emerson’s family history. His father wanted him to be one, too. In 1817, at the age of 14, he began his education at Harvard College. He finished in 1821 and started to teach in a local school. In 1825, he continued studies at Harvard Divinity School to be a minister. By 1829, he was the head of a church in Boston. Then some events happened that made him change the direction of his life. In 1831, his wife died. Soon after that, Emerson left America to go on a journey through Europe. He returned after almost a year, then married again in 1833. Emerson didn't want to continue to be the head of a church. Instead, he began speaking in halls and schools. He began writing his thoughts in short writings and speeches. His first essay was “Nature.” It would become one of his most popular essays. Then, many scholars know about him after he gave a speech at Harvard Divinity School in 1837. Emerson became an author instead of a head of a town church by creating his own, instead of following someone else's, plan for his life. Emerson’s days as a child, when he was the son of a head of a town church, shaped his religious views. He also formed his way of thinking about spiritual topics from his education at Harvard. These views are present in his philosophy of Transcendentalism, a way of thinking about the connections between man, nature, and the highest being. Church leaders of Emerson’s time focused on religious topics. Emerson instead focused on the everyday lives of people. Even though his father died when he was eight, and his first wife died a few years after marriage, Emerson wrote in a good way about his subjects. Samuel Taylor Coleridge, an author who lived during the same time as Emerson, also affected him. Emerson had several effects on Americans during his time. The first effect he had was on the value of the individual. He once wrote, “Let us unfetter ourselves of our historical associations and find a pure standard in the idea of man.” Up to this time, Americans still looked to England and other European countries for ideas on fashion and ways of thinking. Emerson’s writings gave impulse to Americans to be free of European ideas on what is right or good. Along with individualism, Emerson is best known for starting the Transcendentalist movement. This philosophy made important the ideas of self-discovery and the connections between nature, all persons as a group, and the highest being. In his later life, Emerson was a close friend of many other important authors and thinkers, including William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, John Stuart Mill, and Thomas Carlyle. He traveled the world, including France, England, Italy and the Middle East. Emerson was active in writing and speaking into the 1870s. However, he started to forget things. He would only read from detailed notes or scripts. By 1879, his memory was so bad that he stopped making public appearances and speeches. He still socialized at private events, but never with the amount of talking that he once did. Walt Whitman described him at a party in 1881 to be a careful listener but he didn't join in any conversations. Within six months, in early 1882, Emerson died of pneumonia in Concord, Massachusetts.

Johann Gottlieb Fichte (; German: [ˈjoːhan ˈɡɔtliːp ˈfɪçtə]; May 19, 1762 – January 27, 1814), was a German philosopher. He was one of the first philosophers of the movement known as German idealism. He died of typhus in Berlin.

Friedrich Ludwig Gottlob Frege (8 November 1848 – 26 July 1925) was a German mathematician and philosopher. Today, he is remembered for the work he did in mathematical logic and the foundations of first order logic and mathematics. He is generally considered to be the father of analytic philosophy, for his writings on the philosophy of language and mathematics. When he published his works, they were mostly ignored by others of his time. Giuseppe Peano (1858–1932) and Bertrand Russell (1872–1970) introduced his work to later generations of logicians and philosophers. An overview of Frege's writings including English translations, at the university of Berkeley.

Hans-Georg Gadamer (; February 11, 1900 – March 13, 2002) was a German philosopher. His philosophy was about the continental tradition. He was best known for his 1960 magnum opus Truth and Method (Wahrheit und Methode) on hermeneutics.

Jürgen Habermas (18 June 1929 – 14 March 2026) was a German philosopher and sociologist, or someone who studied different societies. He used a type of theory called critical theory, where he studied how people use power. He also used the theory of American pragmatism, which studies if something is true or not by the effects of actions. He is known for his work on the theory of the public sphere. He studied power in democracy, and politics. He also studied how people develop a society through language and communication, and tried to understand how that society and the government work together. Habermas was born in Düsseldorf, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. Habermas lived in Gummersbach, near the city of Cologne until his graduation from gymnasium. He was raised in a Protestant religious family because his grandfather was in charge of the seminary, or religious school, in Gummersbach. Jürgen Habermas went to the universities of Göttingen (1949/50), Zürich (1950/51), and Bonn (1951/54). He earned a doctorate (PhD) from Bonn in 1954 with his work Das Absolute und die Geschichte. Von der Zwiespältigkeit in Schellings Denken (The absolute and history: on the contradiction in Schelling's thought). From 1956 on, he studied philosophy and sociology under the critical theorists Max Horkheimer and Theodor Adorno at the Johann Wolfgang Goethe University in Frankfurt am Main. Because Horkheimer had asked Habermas to make some changes to his dissertation. Habermas did not want to do this, and thought that the Frankfurt School was not correct in its views of modern culture. Habermas left the Frankfurt School (a school of thought rather than one made of bricks and mortar). He finished his habilitation, or highest academic degree, in political science at the University of Marburg under the Marxist Wolfgang Abendroth. His habilitation work was entitled, Strukturwandel der Öffentlichkeit; Untersuchungen zu einer Kategorie der Bürgerlichen Gesellschaft (published in English in 1989 titled The structural transformation of the public sphere: an inquiry into a category of bourgeois society). In 1961, he became a privatdozent in Marburg. He began working as a "extraordinary professor" (professor without a chair) of philosophy at the University of Heidelberg. Hans-Georg Gadamer and Karl Löwith got him this job. In 1964 Habermas returned to Frankfurt to take over Horkheimer's job in philosophy and sociology. He was in charge of the Max Planck Institute in Starnberg (near Munich) in 1971, and worked there until 1983, two years after the publication of his main work, The Theory of Communicative Action. Habermas then returned to his chair at Frankfurt as head of the Institute for Social Research. After retiring from Frankfurt in 1993, Habermas wrote many books and articles. In 1986, he received the Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize of the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft, which is the highest honour awarded in German research. He was a "Permanent Visiting" Professor at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois, and "Theodor Heuss Professor" at The New School, New York. Habermas died in Starnberg, Germany on 14 March 2026, at the age of 96. Habermas was awarded The Prince of Asturias Award in Social Sciences for 2003. Habermas was also the 2004 Kyoto Laureate in the Arts and Philosophy section. He traveled to San Diego and on March 5, 2005, as part of the University of San Diego's Kyoto Symposium, gave a speech entitled The Public Role of Religion in Secular Context, about the Separation of church and state. He received the 2005 Holberg International Memorial Prize (about € 520,000). He was elected a member of the Academia Europaea in 1989.

Edmund Gustav Albrecht Husserl (; April 8, 1859, Prostějov, Moravia, Austrian Empire – April 26, 1938, Freiburg, Germany) was an Austrian-German philosopher and mathematician who is deemed the founder of phenomenology. He broke with the positivist orientation of the science and philosophy of his time, believing that experience is the source of all knowledge. Husserl studied mathematics under Karl Weierstraß, completing a Ph.D. under Leo Königsberger, and studied philosophy under Franz Brentano and Carl Stumpf. Then Husserl taught philosophy, as a Privatdozent at Halle from 1887, and as a professor: then at Freiburg im Breisgau from 1916 until his 1928 retirement. Husserl was born into a Jewish family in a town that was then in the Austrian Empire (after 1918 a part of Czechoslovakia, and since 1993 a part of the Czech Republic). He became a member of the Lutheran Church in 1886. He initially studied mathematics but then started attending lectures on psychology and philosophy. Husserl was so impressed by Brentano that he decided to dedicate his life to philosophy. His major written work is Philosophie der Arithmetik (1891). In these first works he tries to combine mathematics, psychology and philosophy with a main goal to provide a sound foundation for mathematics. He analyzes the psychological process needed to obtain the concept of number and then tries to build up a systematical theory on this analysis. To achieve this he uses several methods and concepts taken from his teachers. From Weierstrass he gets the idea that we generate the concept of number by counting a certain collection of objects. From Brentano and Stumpf he takes over the distinction between proper and improper presenting. In an example Husserl explains this in the following way: if you are standing in front of a house, you have a proper, direct presentation of that house, but if you are looking for it and ask for directions, then these directions (e.g. the house on the corner of this and that street) are an indirect, improper presentation. In other words, you can have a proper presentation of an object if it is actually present, and an improper (or symbolic as he also calls it) if you only can indicate that object through signs, symbols, etc. Another important element that Husserl took over from Brentano is intentionality. It is the notion that the main characteristic of consciousness is that it is always intentional. While often simplistically summarised as "aboutness" or the relationship between mental acts and the external world, Brentano defined it as the main characteristic of mental phenomena, by which they could be distinguished from physical phenomena. Some years after the publication of his main work, the Logische Untersuchungen (Logical Investigations; 1900-1901) Husserl made some key conceptual elaborations which led him to assert that in order to study the structure of consciousness, one would have to distinguish between the act of consciousness and the phenomena at which it is directed (the object-in-itself, transcendent to consciousness). Knowledge of essences would only be possible by "bracketing" all assumptions about the existence of an external world. He called this procedure epoché. Husserl then started to concentrate on the ideal, essential structures of consciousness. The metaphysical problem of establishing what kind of reality we perceive was of little interest to Husserl in spite of his being a transcendental idealist. Husserl proposed that the world of objects and ways in which we direct ourselves toward and perceive those objects is normally conceived of in what he called the "natural standpoint", which is characterized by a belief that objects materially exist and exhibit properties that we see as emanating from them. Husserl proposed a radical new phenomenological way of looking at objects by examining how we in our many ways of being intentionally directed toward them, actually "constitute" them (to be distinguished from materially "creating objects or objects". In a later period, Husserl began to wrestle with the complicated issues of intersubjectivity, specifically, how communication about an object can be assumed to refer to the same ideal entity (Cartesian Meditations, Meditation V). Husserl tries new methods of bringing his readers to understand the importance of phenomenology to scientific observation: specifically he refers to psychology) and what he means for "bracketing natural attitude". The Crisis of the European Sciences is Husserl's unfinished work that deals most directly with these issues. In it, Husserl for the first time attempts a historical overview of the development of Western philosophy and science, emphasizing the challenges presented by their increasingly (one-sidedly) empirical and naturalistic orientation.
